newsitem.title: BELARUS: FEATURE - Chagall's first exhibition in Belarus homeland.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chagall's first exhibition in Belarus homeland.

text.p: Belarus, culturally impoverished after centuries of Russian domination, has a rare chance to bask in national pride this month as masterpieces of its long-forgotten son Marc Chagall go on display for the first time here.
It took Meret Meyer Graber, Chagall's 55-year-old granddaughter, years to bring this former Soviet capital an exhibition of his work.
"We are here. And it's a miracle!" said Meyer Graber, who travelled from her home in Switzerland to attend the opening last week.

Chagall was born Moishe Segal in 1887 in the Belarussian town of Vitebsk. Although Vitebsk became the cradle of the Soviet avant-garde early this century, Chagall joined a stream of intellectuals who fled the Soviet Union after the revolution. He left for Europe in 1922.
The Soviet authorities later banned his art and not one example is permanently on display in the economically troubled land of his birth.

With her bright green clothes, long thin chin and sparkling eyes looking startlingly like Chagall whose self-portrait hung behind her, Meyer Graber told how her family had long dreamed of visiting his homeland.
But the Soviet authorities refused to let them.

"For me it is very important to come and see the landscapes, the warmth, which I have felt since childhood looking at Chagall's paintings. I feel as if Chagall's land is breathing beneath my feet. I recognise it. I am happy," she said.
"Chagall has come home after many years of oblivion," declared Culture Minister Alexander Sosnovsky.
The name of Chagall, who spent his childhood and early adulthood in Vitebsk about 250 km (150 miles) east of the Belarussian capital, Minsk, was never mentioned in textbooks during the Soviet years.

For the first time last week Belarus officially recognised the Jewish emigre, born when no one dared to breathe the word Belarus for fear of offending Russia's imperial authorities who considered it a region of its mighty empire.

Meyer Graber brought eight guaches and four watercolours from Chagall's collection, while 59 lithographs from his Mediterranean period in the 1950s were lent by the Museum of Modern Art in Paris and the Chagall museum in Nice. Chagall spent most of his life in France.

"What's the Mediterranean got to do with it? Every painting has the little old one-storey house of Chagall's Vitebsk!" declared Ilya Reznik, a cinematographer attending the invitation-only opening night.
CHAGALL'S HOME A MUSEUM WITHOUT ONE EXAMPLE OF HIS WORK

Reznik, a devoted follower of Chagall, visited the artist's house in the 1980s before Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika years began -- a building that is only now being transformed into a museum though not a single work is available to go on display.
Reznik recalled how neighbours -- a Jewish family on one side and a police station on the other -- were irritated with fans daring to visit the house, not realising its significance.

"Chagall was banned, but people came to the little yard anyway. The family got fed up with all the visitors. They didn't understand what house they were living in and why we were bothering them," Reznik recalled.
The state poisoned the memory of Chagall even after the artist's death in 1985.

As the Israeli parliament marked the 100th anniversary of his birth, editors of the official encyclopedia of Soviet Belarus were forced to publish an article about him in the anti-Zionist tone for which the Soviet authorities were known.
Irina Shelenkova, who worked on the encyclopedia, took Communist Party leaders to court to defend Chagall but she lost to the conservative communist regime and was sacked.

"I saw how officials had nothing to do with Chagall and how everyone now wants to be linked to his fame. But it is the same party bosses who persecuted his memory then who are in power now," said Yuri Gorulev, a cameraman who made a film about the artist and Belarus 10 years ago.
The film was so taboo it has never been shown, though copies of it were passed from hand-to-hand across the Soviet Union.
"'Chagall is a Zionist and he painted Lenin from the head down,' one of the communist bosses told us -- and in those days that was enough to throw Chagall out of Belarussian history," Gorulev said.
In 1987 party bosses ordered a sculptor to remove Chagall from a tryptich of three artists designed for an exhibition to mark his 100th birthday.

It took until 1992 for a memorial to be put up on the corner of Pokrovskaya Street in Vitebsk, where Chagall worked, painting strange saints, sad clowns and lovers floating on the wings of a dream in the moonlight.
"The town of my childhood where I can enter without visas and passports," Chagall, who died near Nice aged 98 in 1985, wrote of Vitebsk.
